title: Line Down
summary: Bring a valley’s power back in a monsoon storm: find shorts by Ohm’s law, swap a corroded joint and colour-code a pump resistor.
subject: physics
learningOutcome: The student can find R from V and I, locate a short from ohms per km, tell ohmic from non-ohmic traces, use R = ρl/A and the k² rule for a stretched wire, and read the colour code.

levels.title: Find the short
levels.adds: Baseline: R = V/I from the tester, and resistance grows in step with length, so the short is R ÷ (ohms per km) away (Section 3.4).
hints: Resistance is the tester’s voltage divided by its current. Turn milliamps into amperes first.
Every kilometre of line adds the same resistance: distance = R ÷ (ohms per km).
The test current goes out on one wire and back on the other, so a line’s ohms per km count both wires.

levels.title: The corroded joint
levels.adds: New idea: only a part whose V–I graph is a straight line through the origin, the same either way round, obeys Ohm’s law (Section 3.6).
hints: Look at each card: a sound joint gives a straight line through the middle of its axes.
A curve, a line that goes flat on one side, or a straight line that misses the origin all mean V/I changes.
Ohm’s law needs V/I to stay the same at every voltage and in both directions.

levels.title: A different wire
levels.adds: New idea: R = ρl/A, so the ohms per km come from the metal and the cross-section, and half the radius gives four times the resistance (Ex 3.4).
hints: One wire 1 km long has R = ρ × 1000 ÷ A, with A in m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²).
Double it for the loop: the test current goes out and back.
Half the radius is a quarter of the area, so four times the ohms per km.

levels.title: The landslide span
levels.adds: More steps: a span stretched k times at constant volume has k² times its resistance, while the resistivity of the metal stays the same.
hints: k times longer and 1/k of the area: R = ρl/A grows by k × k.
Take the stretched span’s extra resistance off the reading before you divide.
If the reading is less than the line up to the landslide, the short is before it.

levels.title: The burnt resistor
levels.adds: Apply it: Ohm’s law gives the burnt resistor’s value from its volts and milliamps, then set its three colour bands.
hints: R = V/I. Turn the milliamps into amperes first.
The first two bands are digits and the third is the power of ten: how many zeros follow.
Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9.

misconceptions: Resistance depends only on the material
A thinner wire has a lower resistance
Stretching a wire changes the resistivity of the metal
A straight V–I graph always means Ohm’s law holds
